title: The Kind of Science that Teaching Needs
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Stuart distinguishes between two kinds of 'science' in education: a stultifying kind built on theories posing as science and imposed on teachers, and an invigorating kind built on fresh, testable hypotheses that teachers themselves form and pursue. His chief example of the first is the 'Cognitive Hypothesis' that IQ and test performance matter most, which he challenges with anecdote, workshop experience and research on noncognitive factors, and which he says is done to educators rather than inviting them in. He proposes a four-step alternative: permit teachers to form hypotheses, vet them, reward the research work, and require teachers to share results usefully, modeled on Character Lab's Teacher Innovator Grant. Dissecting his own goal-setting 'experiment,' he credits its curricular connection and efficiency but admits he had no hypothesis or measurement, then outlines a properly designed pop-up debate study for the coming year. He concludes that education's science must encourage tinkering and measurement within professional communities rather than proving pet philosophies right.
points: Stuart argues that the 'over-sciencing' wearing teachers down is really philosophy posing as science, imposed on educators rather than inviting them in.
He challenges the Cognitive Hypothesis, the belief that IQ and test scores best predict success, with anecdote, audience experience and research on character.
His remedy is a four-step model: permit teacher hypotheses, vet them, reward the research work, and require practical sharing of results.
Critiquing his own goal-setting activity, he admits that without a defined hypothesis or measurement plan he could not learn whether it was worth ten minutes a week.
He sketches a better-designed study measuring how pop-up debates and film review affect zest, social intelligence and grit.
quotes: The difference between the two sciences is that the living one operates within a world of fresh, testable, adapting hypotheses, whereas the dying one — the one that is killing us as teachers — operates on philosophies and theories posing as science.

And I'm no science teacher, but I know enough of science to know this: You don't do hypotheses to people; you don't do hypotheses at all. That is not the kind of science that makes young people grow up to become science teachers.

I had no plan for measuring the results of the intervention. I can't tell you if this activity was successful or not. I can say that a lot of kids liked it; I can say it gave me some great insight into what makes my students tick.

In short, I was not thinking scientifically. I had no clearly defined hypothesis, and as a result no hope of making this a study I could really learn from. I was doing what great teachers do, but I was missing out on a huge opportunity to learn from what I was doing.

The kind of science education needs cannot be about perfection. It needs to encourage the kinds of quasi-experimentation that I did last year with goal-setting, and it needs to build capacity in teachers to grow into conducting better and smarter research throughout their careers.

Right now, education seems to be stuck in a science that's all about proving that my edu-strategy or philosophy is right; we need to abandon that, instead cultivating a science that promotes inventing, tinkering — and, yes, measuring — within nourishing professional communities and toward Everests much taller than measures of cognitive achievement.
